source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Built 13,465 prompts to test human-like biases (anchoring, framing, status quo, group attribution, primacy) in student-admission decisions. All four models showed bias patterns.
numbers: GPT-4 admitted 40.5% more students under a reject framing than under an admit framing (framing delta -0.405 in admit rate). Llama-2 7B classed 32.1% fewer females as good at math. Models: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Llama-2 7B and 13B.
limits: One task domain (admissions). Status quo bias was not clearly seen. Prompt-induced bias is partly a prompt-sensitivity effect.
agent_relevance: Biases in an LLM are cheap to induce with wording alone. A test needs a paired neutral-versus-biased prompt design.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Zero-shot awareness prompts gave only small gains. Few-shot debiasing (contrastive and counterfactual examples) often broke the model.
numbers: Few-shot made some models answer admit or reject almost 100% of the time (Llama-2 7B contrastive: 0.996 and 1.000 admission rates). GPT-4 framing gap with awareness -0.470, contrastive -0.410, counterfactual -0.570 versus -0.405 baseline: no gain.
quote: few-shot debiasing introduces substantial additional context that drastically changes the prompt
limits: Failure was an instruction-following collapse, not just residual bias. Small models hit it hardest.
agent_relevance: Confirms schema 4b: telling the model to avoid bias does not fix it, and added examples can cause new errors. Do not add debias exemplars.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Self-help debiasing (the model rewrites the biased prompt itself) worked best, mainly for high-capacity models. Low-capacity models changed many decisions when allowed to revise.
numbers: With self-help, GPT-4 biased group-attribution prompt elements fell to 0% and framing elements to 2.7%. Llama models changed 40-52% of anchoring decisions between the sequential and self-help setups. GPT-3.5 cut group-attribution prompt bias by only 8.9%.
limits: Works by removing the biasing text from the input, not by changing how the model reasons. Needs a capable model.
agent_relevance: Closest analogue to a structural fix: strip or restructure the biasing input rather than ask for neutrality. Supports a neutral-restatement step at S1 that code can enforce.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: SACD loops three steps on the prompt: find biased sentences, analyse the bias, rewrite the prompt. It repeats until none are found. It beat CoT, few-shot, Reflexion, multi-agent debate, zero-shot and self-help debiasing on finance (FOMC), medical (PubMedQA) and legal (LegalBench) decisions.
numbers: Average bias score range for SACD 0.0300-0.1570 (FOMC), 0.0425-0.1790 (PubMedQA), 0.0400-0.1235 (LegalBench) across four LLMs, versus best baselines 0.0625-0.3490, 0.0725-0.4175, 0.0725-0.2625. Single-bias and multi-bias (anchoring, bandwagon, loss aversion) settings.
limits: Biases were injected into prompts by the authors, so it measures susceptibility to planted cues. It costs several extra model calls per item. Bias score is not accuracy.
agent_relevance: A code-controlled rewrite loop that cleans cues from the input. Fits the schema idea that code runs the loop and the model fills one slot (rewrite). Test at equal tokens (G7).

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Iterating mattered. In finance the first SACD pass was no better than baselines; later passes were.
numbers: Finance bias score by iteration 0.2070, 0.1460, 0.1175 versus vanilla 0.1648, CoT 0.2220, self-help 0.1885. Medical 0.2260, 0.1610, 0.1585 versus vanilla 0.6655, CoT 0.5440, self-help 0.2880. Legal 0.1230, 0.0970, 0.0965 versus vanilla 0.3840, CoT 0.2470, self-help 0.4590.
limits: In finance the first pass was worse than vanilla. Gains flatten after pass 2-3.
agent_relevance: Run the rewrite loop a small fixed number of passes and stop when a detector returns none (a signal, as G1 wants), not on a schedule.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Reflection-style and debate methods amplified bias in multi-bias prompts. Few-shot debiasing was inconsistent. Self-help was the strongest baseline but weak on multi-bias prompts.
numbers: Multi-agent debate scored 0.5155 on FOMC with gpt-3.5-turbo; Reflexion 0.5585 on PubMedQA with llama3.1-70b-instruct; few-shot debiasing often above 0.5 and up to above 0.8. Self-help on LegalBench llama3.1-8b multi-bias: 0.2300. CoT averaged 0.2470-0.6150.
quote: these methods learn from biased feedback or engage with other biased agents
limits: Authors explain amplification as agents learning from biased feedback; this is their interpretation, not tested by ablation.
agent_relevance: Supports G9 (no debate): debate and reflection copy the planted bias across agents.

source: Lyu et al. (2025) Self-Adaptive Cognitive Debiasing for LLMs in Decision-Making (SACD)
finding: Error analysis of the debiasers: the older self-help approach mostly under-debiased; SACD mostly confused bias types.
numbers: Total errors out of 500 per domain: finance self-help 257 (51.4%) vs SACD 61 (12.2%); medical 209 (41.8%) vs 111 (22.2%); legal 409 (81.8%) vs 79 (15.8%).
limits: Counts from the authors' own audit of failed cases.
agent_relevance: The detect-then-rewrite split gives a measurable failure taxonomy (misjudged, confused, insufficient). A check step can log which stage failed.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Benchmark of four bias families (Judgment, Information Processing, Social, Response). All three models were biased in all four families. A prompt-level debiasing instruction fixed Response bias but made Judgment bias worse.
numbers: Baseline: judgment shift 4.3 pp (GPT-4o-mini), 7.7 pp (Llama-3.3-70B), 2.7 pp (Qwen2.5-72B); order bias 30%, 56%, 66%; first-option pick 77-79% versus 36.8% chance. Debias prompt effect: Response +40.5%, Social +5.9%, Info Processing -1.1%, Judgment -4.4% (backfires).
quote: prompt-level debiasing substantially reduces Response biases but backfires for Judgment biases
limits: Three models, one prompt wording per family; cross-family metrics are not comparable. Under-review preprint.
agent_relevance: Direct 2026 evidence for 4b: a debiasing instruction is not safe for judgment biases. Instruction effect must be measured per bias before use.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Per-bias breakdown: the same debias instruction helped some judgment biases and hurt others.
numbers: Helped: illusion of control +7.0, in-group bias +6.6, framing effect +5.8, risk compensation +4.5 points. Hurt: fundamental attribution error -21.0, hyperbolic discounting -13.4 (42.8% biased baseline), with the worst rows near -19.6 points; the disposition effect (82.4% biased) is also in the backfire list.
limits: Averaged over three models. The table was partly garbled in text extraction, so only clearly legible rows are quoted.
agent_relevance: Instructions work on cues the model can name; they fail or invert where the bias sits in numeric or value computation. Put those checks in code.

source: Huang et al. (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Activation steering cut bias scores by 26-32% on open models while keeping most capability. This is a non-prompt route. Probes show biases are linearly readable inside the model.
numbers: Bias score (fraction biased) reduced 26-32%; capability on 25 benchmarks: Llama negligible loss, Qwen up to -19.0 pp for Judgment biases. Cross-model steering rates correlate r(246)=.621, p<.001; bias directions nearly orthogonal across models (cosine 0.01).
limits: Needs weights access; our agent is scaffold-only. Capability cost on Qwen is large.
agent_relevance: Not usable in a prompt-only scaffold, but it shows the effect is model-internal, which is why wording cannot reach it.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The Bias is in the Details: An Assessment of Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Eight biases across 45 LLMs and over 2.8 million responses. Every model showed bias on a large share of items. Larger models were less biased only some of the time.
numbers: Bias-consistent behaviour in 17.8-57.3% of instances. Size over 32B reduced bias in 39.5% of cases; models above 32B showed diminishing benefit.
limits: Single-turn prompts at temperature 1.0; automated scoring of answers.
agent_relevance: Scale is not a reliable debiaser. Do not assume the base model has solved these.

source: Knipper et al. (2025) The Bias is in the Details: An Assessment of Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Prompt detail (TELeR levels) changed bias, but not always downward. Prompts that say be objective and reason logically helped; extra context sometimes made bias cues stick.
numbers: Levels 3-4 (explicit rationality instructions) raised bias resistance by 6.5-14.9%. Overattribution resistance fell 8.2% going from Level 1 to 2; Representativeness fell 4.6%. Reasoning models (QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1) resisted Framing more, but not other biases.
limits: Gains are per-bias and modest; some added details hurt. Not a general instruction effect.
agent_relevance: Set beside the CogBias result: instructions give single-digit to low-double-digit shifts in either direction. Treat as unreliable unless a check confirms it.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: On 62 questions from the Play-the-Future human dataset, GPT-4 and GPT-4o were pulled toward numeric anchor hints. Four simple mitigations did not help.
numbers: Anchoring index about 0.45 for GPT-4 versus 0.61 in the human study. CoT, thoughts of principles, ignore-the-anchor, and reflection each gave no significant improvement (t-test p-values on biased answers stayed very small) on GPT-4 and GPT-4o. Weaker GPT-3.5 varied more.
quote: simple algorithms such as Chain-of-Thought, Thoughts of Principles, Ignoring Anchor Hints, and Reflection are not sufficient
limits: Two main models. Single numeric-estimate task. Anchoring index is computed differently from the human paper, so 0.45 versus 0.61 is approximate.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to ignore the anchor fails, as it does in humans. A direct 4b confirmation for anchoring.

source: Lou and Sun (2024) Anchoring Bias in Large Language Models: An Experimental Study
finding: What did work: show both a low and a high anchor (the human advice to consider the other anchor). Answers moved close to the bias-free value for questions whose two anchors bracketed the true value.
numbers: With Both-Anchor on GPT-4, 8 of 15 plotted questions (nos. 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15) landed near the bias-free value; the rest still deviated.
limits: Works only when the anchors bracket the truth. Anchors are the authors' own. Small question set.
agent_relevance: A structure-based fix that code can enforce: generate opposing anchors or reference classes and present all at once. This is consider-the-opposite as a data change, not an instruction.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors)
finding: SynAnchors dataset: anchoring is common in LLMs (22-61% of questions anchored), shallow (acts in early layers), and mildest in reasoning models.
numbers: Total anchoring ratio: Llama-3.1-8B 34.7%, Qwen2.5-7B 40.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%, Phi-3.5-mini 46.3%, Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%.
limits: Causal tracing only on Llama-3.1-8B. Dataset was synthesised by DeepSeek-R1, which may share biases with the tested reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-time compute lowers anchoring but does not remove it; one in four items still anchored in the best model.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Understanding the Anchoring Effect of LLM with Synthetic Data (SynAnchors)
finding: Mitigation tests on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B: most conventional fixes did little or made it worse. A two-phase 'set your standard first, then answer' method (Anti-DP) helped on Llama.
numbers: Llama total anchoring 34.7% base; question-aware prompt 36.8%; knowledge enhancement 50.5% (worse); self-improving 38.4%; adversarial LoRA finetune 33.3%; DoLa 37.5-38.5%; Anti-DP 24.7%. Qwen 40.0% base; question-aware 43.0%; self-improving 48.0%; Anti-DP 40.8%. Authors: up to 10% alleviation.
quote: Mitigation strategies achieved up to a 10% alleviation in anchoring effects, confirming the failure of elimination
limits: Small models, one run per cell. Anti-DP did not help Qwen on numeric items. Finetuning helped little.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to think carefully raised anchoring on both models, and a second look (self-improving) raised it on both. Supports G1 and G2: no second look without real output.

source: Itzhak et al. (2024) Instructed to Bias: Instruction-Tuned Language Models Exhibit Emergent Cognitive Bias
finding: Instruction tuning and RLHF increased certainty and belief bias compared with base models. Decoy bias also rose for Mistral.
numbers: Certainty-effect bias score: DaVinci-002 0.24, DaVinci-003 (RLHF) 0.67. Belief-invalid: DaVinci 0.00, DaVinci-002 0.55, DaVinci-003 0.65. Belief-valid 0.00, 0.19, 0.21. Mistral decoy-expensive 0.03 -> Mistral-Instruct 0.24. GPT-4: belief valid 0.07, belief invalid 0.49, logic accuracy 84%.
quote: Models fine-tuned using IT and RLHF show a higher bias than their pretrained counterparts
limits: Table text was partly garbled by extraction, so only unambiguous cells are listed. OpenAI training is unknown, so the RLHF cause is not isolated. Some decoy cells go the other way.
agent_relevance: Alignment training can make some biases larger, so a stronger tuned model is not automatically safer on these tasks.

source: Itzhak et al. (2024) Instructed to Bias: Instruction-Tuned Language Models Exhibit Emergent Cognitive Bias
finding: Mitigation by examples: examples from the same task cut belief bias less than examples that only matched the format. In the GPT family higher logic accuracy came with higher bias score.
numbers: Figure-level result on DaVinci-003 with 1 to 3 shots; no single headline number.
limits: The authors note fine-tuning on bias data is hard to control and may harm common sense.
agent_relevance: Examples that teach the logic carry the bias with them; format-only cues were safer.

source: Itzhak, Belinkov, Stanovsky (2025) Planted in Pretraining, Swayed by Finetuning
finding: Cross-tuning test over 32 cognitive biases: swapping instruction data between OLMo-7B and T5-11B showed bias patterns follow the pretrained backbone more than the finetuning data.
numbers: 32 biases; 3 random seeds per model; 4 main models (OLMo-Flan, OLMo-Tulu, T5-Flan, T5-Tulu) plus community Llama2-7B and Mistral-7B. Clustering by pretraining model beat clustering by instruction data. Seed-level bias SD slightly above MMLU SD. Seed-mean vs original-model bias correlation 0.49 (OLMo) and 0.59 (T5).
limits: LoRA finetuning. Two main backbones. Moderate seed correlation means a bias score from a single run is noisy.
agent_relevance: Biases are set before we touch the model, so a scaffold cannot count on training to fix them. Use repeated samples when scoring bias.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: Cognitive Reflection Test items (150 tasks) and semantic illusions: early GPT-3 models gave the intuitive wrong answer like people. ChatGPT and GPT-4 mostly did not.
numbers: Intuitive-wrong share: GPT-3 davinci-003 80%, humans 55%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, GPT-4 0%. Correct: davinci-003 5%, humans 38%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, GPT-4 96%. Human sample difficulty check: 38% correct versus 41% in the original study (n=3,428).
limits: Newer models may have seen CRT-like items in training. The 'hyperrational' claim rests on CRT-style tasks only.
agent_relevance: The classic bias tasks are now easy for frontier models. Test new variants, not famous items.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi, Kosinski (2023) Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
finding: A reasoning suffix cut the intuitive error of davinci-003; forbidding reasoning barely hurt ChatGPT. A few worked examples of the same form taught the intuition.
numbers: Suffix 'Let's use algebra': intuitive errors 80% -> 29%, correct 5% -> 28%, atypical 15% -> 43%. Forcing a shortest answer: ChatGPT-3.5 correct unchanged (delta -4%, p=.49); GPT-4 correct 95% -> 88%, intuitive 0% -> 10%. Davinci-003 with solved examples in the prompt: CRT type 2 accuracy 2% -> 92% after 2 examples; type 3 12% -> 92% after 7; type 1 0% -> 78% after 30.
limits: Few-shot gains are on tasks of identical form, so they may be pattern copying and not debiasing.
agent_relevance: Structure (a forced reasoning step, same-form worked examples) moved results far more than saying be careful. Same-form worked examples are the fix that worked here.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 (davinci) answered 12 of 12 standard vignettes correctly or with human-like mistakes, and reproduced three of six Kahneman and Tversky prospect-theory effects. Small wording changes broke it.
numbers: Framing, certainty and probability-overweighting effects found; three others not found. All three CRT items answered intuitively wrong. Adversarial vignettes gave non-human-like errors (Cab problem stated 15% blue, model said 20%; a CRT item with the premise changed still got the old answer). Below human performance on the vignette set (t(29134)=-11.50, p<.001).
limits: GPT-3 (2022), pre-ChatGPT. Main tests at temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Matches human biases on famous items and fails on perturbed items. A bias test must use perturbations, as the scaffold's G3 does.

source: Koo et al. (2024) Benchmarking Cognitive Biases in LLMs as Evaluators (COBBLER)
finding: Sixteen LLMs acting as judges showed order, salience, egocentric (self-preference), compassion-fade and bandwagon biases in about 40% of comparisons.
numbers: About 40% of comparisons were biased; model-human agreement (RBO) averaged 44%. Order bias: 11 of 15 models drawn to the first or last position. Models over 100B preferred their own output over 50% of the time under anonymised aliases; with real names the smaller size groups' self-preference rose, KOALA +100%.
limits: 50 instructions, 750 sampled pairs for the human check. Judge task, not a decision task.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: the judge sees no authorship, and order is randomised in code. Order and self-preference are enforceable by code, not by instruction.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Asking a model to review its own answer without outside feedback lowered accuracy. Gains in earlier papers came from using the correct answer to decide when to revise.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 after one self-correct round; GSM8K 75.9 -> 74.7 after two rounds; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 89.0, CSQA 82.0 -> 80.0, HotpotQA 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle labels GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CSQA 75.8 -> 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Intrinsic self-correction only. With tools or code feedback it can work. Table layout was ambiguous in extraction; the main drops are clear.
agent_relevance: This is the structural twin of an 'be aware of bias, check again' instruction. Supports G2: revise only from real output.

source: Turpin et al. (2023) Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think
finding: Planted biasing features (answer order and a suggested answer) lowered chain-of-thought accuracy while the written reasoning never mentioned them. Models wrote explanations that justify the biased answer.
numbers: Accuracy dropped by up to 36% across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks. Same unfaithful pattern on BBQ social-bias items.
quote: Adding biasing features heavily influences model CoT predictions on BBH tasks
limits: GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 era models. Biasing features were artificial.
agent_relevance: CoT neither removes bias nor reveals it (G10). Asking the model to explain its bias is not a check.

source: Weerasekara, Kamarthi, Isaacs (2026) Conditional Cognitive Biases in LLMs: How Biased User Turns Modulate In-Context Reasoning
finding: In 24,300 prompts over a 9 x 9 bias matrix, putting a biased user turn before the task raised bias in 6 of 8 models. A neutral user turn alone already raised it.
numbers: Zero-shot bias magnitude 0.342 (Gemma-2-9B) to 0.437 (Phi-4). Biased turn effect +0.022 to +0.051 in 6 of 8 models (all p<0.001); GPT-4o about 0; Claude-3.5-Haiku -0.064. Neutral turn alone: +0.086 for Llama-3.1-8B (about 25% of baseline), positive in 7 of 8 models. Content effect negative (suppression) for 5 models; DeepSeek-V3 +0.009 and Claude-3.5-Haiku +0.037. Only planning fallacy rose in every model.
limits: Eight models, jury-validated prompts, difference-in-differences. The planning-fallacy result may reflect the prompt template.
agent_relevance: The conversation history an agent carries is itself a bias source. Keeping each step's context clean is a control that code can enforce.

source: Investigating the Impact of LLM Personality on Cognitive Bias Manifestation in Automated Decision-Making Tasks (2025)
finding: The awareness prompt 'Be mindful of not being biased by cognitive bias' was tested across personality-prompted models. Its effect depended on the personality prompt and the model, and was sometimes negative.
numbers: Six biases prevalent (anchoring, decoy, endowment, framing, risk aversion, status quo); sunk cost and group attribution minimal. Example GPT-4o mitigation values: framing +0.126 with conscientiousness, anchoring +0.065 with agreeableness, many cells near zero and some about -0.1.
limits: Small deltas, several models; personality prompts are a confound. Table partly garbled.
agent_relevance: The same debias sentence gives opposite signs under different personas. Do not rely on one debias sentence.

source: Do Language Models Exhibit the Same Cognitive Biases in Problem Solving as Human Learners? (2024)
finding: Tested LLMs on generated word problems in three steps (comprehension, planning, execution). Found human-like biases in comprehension and planning, but not in execution, with and without instruction tuning.
numbers: Neuro-symbolic generated problems with controlled features; no headline number extracted by us.
limits: Abstract and method read; numbers not extracted. Focus is learning science, not debiasing.
agent_relevance: Marginal. LLM errors follow problem structure the way children's do, so item variants can expose them.

source: Heuristics and Biases in AI Decision-Making: Implications for Responsible AGI (2024)
finding: 1,500 experiments over nine biases on GPT-4o, Gemma 2 and Llama 3.1. GPT-4o was best overall; Llama 3.1 relied on heuristics and contradicted itself.
numbers: 1,500 experiments, nine biases (e.g. sunk cost, prospect theory); no per-bias table extracted by us.
limits: Abstract and introduction read; results section not fully checked. Weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Per-model bias profiles differ, so measure our own model.
